n11-licao-projetos.enunciado:
Each project has 5 stages. Each stage starts from your files from the previous stage (if you did it; if not, from the reference solution) and asks for something new: a concept, a defect a coworker left for you to find, a decision. The last stage of each project is a ticket: just the request and the acceptance criteria, no step-by-step. The tests apply all the files to a fresh cluster, so everything you’ve built has to keep working.

  • The full store: API, Redis, the storefront and the way in through the Ingress.
  • The blog with a database: Secret, a StatefulSet with a disk and the backup.
  • Zero-downtime deploy: readiness, rolling update, the rollout deadline, a PDB and the liveness and startup probes.
  • Canary: two versions, the traffic split through the Gateway API and the promotion.
  • Black Friday: requests and limits, the HPA under load, the quota, OOMKilled and the LimitRange.
  • Multi-team: one namespace per team, RBAC (ClusterRole and the view role) and NetworkPolicy.
  • Hardening: no root, Pod Security, a read-only disk, least access and a closed network.
  • Dev and prod: the same store in two environments, with Helm (with rollback) and with Kustomize.

A tip from people who do this every day: kubectl apply -f ., kubectl get all and kubectl describe solve almost everything. When you get stuck, the Solution tab has the reference for each stage.
n11-licao-projetos.vidaReal: Until now, each mission was a single room. Now it’s the whole construction job: foundation, walls, plumbing and finishing, one stage after another.
n11-licao-projetos.limite: On a real job, nobody rebuilds the foundation at every stage. Here, the tests set everything up again on a clean cluster: whatever you forgot in one stage shows up in the next.

n11-loja-1.titulo: The API and its phone extension
n11-loja-1.enunciado: api.yaml has the API Deployment with 1 replica. Bump it to 2 replicas and add the api Service (port 80, to the pods’ 8080).
n11-loja-1.dica: replicas: 2 and, in the same file after a ---, the Service with selector app: api, port 80 and targetPort 8080.
n11-loja-1.vidaReal: First, the service counter (the API) and the fixed phone extension to reach it.
n11-loja-1.limite: The phone extension only exists for people inside the condo: from outside, nobody can get in yet.

testes.descricao: the API answers on its phone extension

n11-loja-2.titulo: The phone extension that doesn’t ring
n11-loja-2.enunciado: A coworker wrote redis.yaml (the Redis Deployment and Service). Redis is up, but the redis phone extension doesn’t lead anywhere. Find out why and fix it. Then tell the API where the cache is: the REDIS_HOST=redis variable.
n11-loja-2.dica: kubectl get endpoints redis shows <none>: compare the Service’s selector with the pods’ labels (kubectl get pods --show-labels). On the API: env: [{ name: REDIS_HOST, value: redis }].
n11-loja-2.vidaReal: The API gets a fridge (Redis) so it doesn’t have to fetch everything from the stockroom every time. But the fridge’s phone extension rings in an empty room.
n11-loja-2.limite: The Service doesn’t check whether its selector makes sense: a selector that matches no pod is accepted without an error, and the extension just stays silent.

testes.descricao: the API knows where the cache is, and the extension reaches it

n11-loja-3.enunciado: vitrine.yaml has nginx and the vitrine (storefront) Service, but the pods never leave ContainerCreating. Find out what’s missing (kubectl describe pod tells you) and fix it: the storefront page has to say Loja do kube-learn.
n11-loja-3.dica: The pod’s events say: configmap "vitrine-html" not found. Create that ConfigMap with an index.html key: the volume becomes the /usr/share/nginx/html folder, and each key becomes a file.
n11-loja-3.vidaReal: The storefront (nginx) shows the page pinned on the bulletin board (the ConfigMap). Without the board, it doesn’t even open its door.
n11-loja-3.limite: The kubelet waits for the ConfigMap to show up and retries on its own: as soon as you create it, the pod starts, no need to delete anything.

testes.descricao: the storefront shows the page

n11-loja-4.enunciado: entrada.yaml sends loja.local to the storefront. Add the API’s entrance: everything that starts with /api (/api, /api/carrinho...) goes to the api Service; everything else stays with the storefront.
n11-loja-4.dica: One more item in paths: path /api, backend service api, port 80. The pathType decides the “everything that starts with”: Prefix matches /api and /api/carrinho; Exact, only /api.
n11-loja-4.vidaReal: The front gate’s front desk: whoever asks for “loja.local” goes to the storefront; whoever asks for “/api” goes to the API counter.
n11-loja-4.limite: The Ingress picks the longest path: /api beats / for anyone asking for /api/anything.

testes.descricao: the store opens from outside

msgs.3: loja.local/api/carrinho reaches the API (the 404 is the API’s, not nginx’s)

n11-loja-5.enunciado:
Tomorrow the store opens to the public. I don’t want any customer seeing an error when we switch the API’s version, and the management office wants to know how much each API clerk uses.

Marta, who owns the store

Acceptance criteria. The how is up to you; some of the criteria are checked by hidden tests.

  • Switching the API’s version (to kubelearn/loja:2.1-aquece, which spends 20 seconds warming up before it serves) leaves no request unanswered.
  • Each API pod reserves (requests) 100m of CPU and 64Mi of memory.
  • The storefront only gets visitors once nginx already answers on /.
  • Everything that already worked keeps working: loja.local and loja.local/api open from outside.
n11-loja-5.dica: What decides whether a pod gets customers is the readinessProbe; what it reserves goes in resources.requests. Try the switch yourself: kubectl set image deployment/api api=kubelearn/loja:2.1-aquece and kubectl get pods -w.
n11-loja-5.vidaReal: Before opening the doors: the building manager checks who’s ready, and each clerk says how much power they need.
n11-loja-5.limite: The readinessProbe only protects you if the answer is honest: a /healthz that always says ok protects against nothing.

testes.descricao: the store still opens from outside
the API reserves CPU and memory
the storefront only serves once it’s ready
the API switches versions without anyone going unanswered

n11-blog-1.enunciado: segredo.yaml has the empty banco (database) Secret. Put the senha (password) key in it (any value you like).
n11-blog-1.vidaReal: Before calling in the database, the sealed envelope with the password.
n11-blog-1.limite: Sealed isn’t a safe: anyone who can read Secrets in the namespace can read the password (it’s just base64).

testes.descricao: the envelope has the password

n11-blog-2.titulo: The database that won’t come up
n11-blog-2.enunciado: banco.yaml has the db StatefulSet (postgres), but db-0 keeps crashing and restarting. Its logs say what’s missing: give it that read from the banco Secret (no password written in the YAML). Also create the headless Service db (port 5432), which gives each apartment a fixed address (db-0.db).
n11-blog-2.dica: kubectl logs db-0: POSTGRES_PASSWORD is missing. env with valueFrom.secretKeyRef (name: banco, key: senha) and a Service with clusterIP: None.
n11-blog-2.vidaReal: The database’s apartment 0, with a fixed number, and the list with each apartment’s direct extension (the headless Service), which calls it by name.
n11-blog-2.limite: Headless doesn’t spread the calls around: it only gives out each apartment’s address (db-0.db).

testes.descricao: the database is up

n11-blog-3.enunciado: Give the database its own disk: a volumeClaimTemplates dados (data) of 1Gi, mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data.
n11-blog-3.dica: volumeClaimTemplates in the StatefulSet spec and the volumeMount with the same name (dados).
n11-blog-3.vidaReal: Apartment 0 gets its own storage unit in the garage: if the resident changes, the unit keeps its stuff.
n11-blog-3.limite: Deleting the StatefulSet doesn’t delete the storage unit (the PVC): the data stays until someone deletes the PVC.

testes.descricao: the database has its own disk
db-0 comes back with the same disk (and the data)

msgs.0: the file written earlier is still there

n11-blog-4.enunciado: A coworker wrote blog.yaml: the blog Deployment (with DB_HOST and DB_SENHA) and the blog Service. But the pods stay in CreateContainerConfigError, and kubectl logs shows nothing. Find out why and fix it.
n11-blog-4.dica: No container, no log: the reason is in the events (kubectl describe pod). Compare the key the blog asks for with the keys the banco Secret has (kubectl describe secret banco).
n11-blog-4.vidaReal: The blog calls the database at apartment 0’s fixed address, with the password from the envelope. Except they asked for the envelope by the wrong name.
n11-blog-4.limite: Without the key in the Secret, the container never even gets created: there’s no log to read, only the pod’s events.

testes.descricao: the blog finds the database

msgs.4: DB_SENHA comes from the banco Secret

n11-blog-5.enunciado:
The blog has become the heart of the company, and nobody sleeps well without a backup. The intern left a draft in backup.yaml, but it runs every minute and, from what I saw, it doesn’t even work.

Rui, from finance

Acceptance criteria. The how is up to you; some of the criteria are checked by hidden tests.

  • The backup runs every day at 2 AM, Sao Paulo time (the cluster’s clock is in UTC).
  • A backup never starts while the previous one is still running.
  • A backup started by hand (kubectl create job teste --from=cronjob/backup-db) finishes successfully.
  • The database password comes from the banco Secret: no password written in the YAML.
n11-blog-5.dica: The fields are in kubectl explain cronjob.spec (schedule, timeZone, concurrencyPolicy). To watch the draft fail: kubectl create job teste --from=cronjob/backup-db and kubectl logs job/teste.
n11-blog-5.vidaReal: Every night, at 2 AM, someone copies the database into the safe: one copy at a time, with the password from the envelope.
n11-blog-5.limite: A backup that’s never been tested isn’t a backup: run the Job by hand every now and then.

testes.descricao: the schedule: every day at 2 AM Sao Paulo time, one backup at a time
the backup started by hand finishes successfully
the password comes from the banco Secret

msgs.0: the backup reads the password from the banco Secret

n11-zero-1.enunciado: loja.yaml has the store (4 replicas) and its phone extension. The next version, kubelearn/loja:2.1-aquece, spends 20 seconds warming up before it serves, and the extension sends customers to it anyway. Make the extension only send customers to whoever already answers on /healthz (port 8080). The hidden tests make that version switch with a client hitting the store every second.
n11-zero-1.vidaReal: The store’s new version takes 20 seconds to warm up. Without asking whether it’s ready, the phone extension sends customers to clerks still tying their aprons.
n11-zero-1.limite: Readiness doesn’t speed anything up: the clerk still takes just as long, they just don’t get anyone before they’re ready.

testes.descricao: the probe is in place
the warming-up version doesn’t drop anyone

n11-zero-2.enunciado: With the Deployment’s default (25% may leave before the new one is ready), a version switch leaves the store with 3 ready pods for a while. The store needs 4 all the time: configure the rolling update to never drop below 4 ready, swapping one at a time.
n11-zero-2.dica: spec.strategy: { type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 } }: open a new one before closing an old one.
n11-zero-2.vidaReal: In a step-by-step renovation, a new apartment opens before an old one closes: never fewer than 4 open.
n11-zero-2.limite: Without room for the extra apartment (the maxSurge), the renovation stalls: maxUnavailable 0 needs spare capacity in the cluster.

testes.descricao: the strategy is in place
the update never goes below 4

n11-zero-3.enunciado: kubelearn/loja:2.0-bugada breaks as soon as it starts. With your strategy, the store doesn’t go down (the old ones keep serving), but the rollout hangs, and kubectl rollout status only gives up after 10 minutes. Make the Deployment declare the rollout failed after 60 seconds without progress.
n11-zero-3.dica: The field is spec.progressDeadlineSeconds (the default is 600). To see it: kubectl set image deployment/loja loja=kubelearn/loja:2.0-bugada, kubectl rollout status deployment/loja and, to go back, kubectl rollout undo deployment/loja.
n11-zero-3.vidaReal: Version 2.0 came with a factory defect: the first new apartment won’t open. The old ones hold the fort, but someone has to announce that the job is stuck.
n11-zero-3.limite: The deadline only marks the rollout as failed (kubectl rollout status exits with an error); it doesn’t undo anything. Going back is up to you: kubectl rollout undo.

testes.descricao: the deadline is in place
the defective version is declared failed, and nobody goes unanswered

msgs.0: the Deployment marks the rollout as failed (ProgressDeadlineExceeded)

n11-zero-4.enunciado: A coworker created pdb.yaml to protect the store, and now kubectl drain node-1 never finishes. Find out why and adjust the PodDisruptionBudget: the maintenance has to move along, without the store dropping below 3 ready pods.
n11-zero-4.dica: kubectl get pdb: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS 0 blocks any drain. With 4 replicas, minAvailable: 3 (or maxUnavailable: 1) lets them leave one at a time. To test: kubectl drain node-1 --ignore-daemonsets and, afterward, kubectl uncordon node-1.
n11-zero-4.vidaReal: The management office is going to renovate the node-1 building and asked the residents to move out (the drain). A coworker promised nobody would ever leave, and the renovation can’t start.
n11-zero-4.limite: The PDB only covers planned departures (drain, eviction): a power outage in the building doesn’t ask for permission.

testes.descricao: the drain of node-1 finishes, without the store dropping below 3

msgs.1: the PDB guarantees at least 3 ready pods

n11-zero-5.enunciado:
Let’s launch 1.1. And, after last week’s scare (a version froze in the middle of the night and stayed up, serving nobody, until someone woke up), I want the store to take care of itself.

Marta, who owns the store

Acceptance criteria. The how is up to you; some of the criteria are checked by hidden tests.

  • The 4 clerks run kubelearn/loja:1.1, and kubectl rollout history deployment/loja tells the reason for the change (with "1.1" in the text).
  • A clerk that freezes (port open, no answer; kubelearn/loja:2.2-trava does that after 40 seconds) is restarted automatically.
  • kubelearn/loja:3.0-lenta, which spends 45 seconds migrating the database before it serves, manages to come up without being killed halfway.
  • Everything that already held keeps holding: no version switch leaves a request unanswered or drops below 4 ready pods.
n11-zero-5.dica: The reason goes in the Deployment’s kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation. What restarts the frozen one is the livenessProbe; what gives the slow start time is the startupProbe (until it passes, the liveness doesn’t even begin).
n11-zero-5.vidaReal: The renovation gets a sign (“version 1.1”) so everyone knows what changed. And the building manager wants to sleep: whoever freezes is restarted automatically, and whoever is slow to open isn’t evicted in the middle of the move.
n11-zero-5.limite: The livenessProbe restarts, it doesn’t fix: a version that always freezes will always restart. The fix is to roll the version back.

testes.descricao: version 1.1, with the reason in the history

msgs.2: the rollout history shows the reason, with 1.1

testes.descricao: whoever freezes is restarted automatically

msgs.0: the kubelet restarted the frozen clerks

testes.descricao: the slow version comes all the way up, with nobody going unanswered
the warming-up version doesn’t drop anyone either

n11-canario-1.enunciado: v1.yaml has loja-v1 (3 replicas, labels app: loja and versao: v1). Create the loja-v1 Service that selects only the v1 pods.
n11-canario-1.vidaReal: The usual store, with the version tag on each apartment’s door.
n11-canario-1.limite: The versao label is just a tag: Kubernetes doesn’t know what a version is; the selectors are what use it.

testes.descricao: v1 answers on its own phone extension

n11-canario-2.titulo: The phone extension that mixes them up
n11-canario-2.enunciado: v2.yaml has loja-v2 (version 1.1, 1 replica, versao: v2) and its phone extension, the loja-v2 Service. But whoever calls loja-v2 sometimes lands on version 1.0. Find out why and fix it, without touching v1.
n11-canario-2.dica: kubectl get endpoints loja-v2 shows 4 pods: the selector app: loja matches v1 too. Add versao: v2 to the selector.
n11-canario-2.vidaReal: A single apartment with the new renovation, to see if anyone complains before renovating the whole building. But its phone extension rings in every one of the store’s apartments.
n11-canario-2.limite: A label is a tag, not an owner: a Service picks any pod whose labels match its selector, whatever Deployment it came from.

testes.descricao: each version with its own phone extension

n11-canario-3.enunciado: rota.yaml sends everything from loja.local to v1. Send about 10% of the visitors to loja-v2, and the rest stays on loja-v1.
n11-canario-3.dica: Each backendRef gets a weight, and the weights are relative (they don’t have to add up to 100): 9 and 1 is the same as 90 and 10. backendRefs: [{ name: loja-v1, port: 80, weight: 90 }, { name: loja-v2, port: 80, weight: 10 }]
n11-canario-3.vidaReal: The sign at the front gate sends 1 in every 10 visitors to the renovated apartment.
n11-canario-3.limite: The weight is per connection, not per person: the same customer may land on one version now and the other later.

testes.descricao: about 10% reach version 1.1

n11-canario-4.enunciado: Switch the split to 50/50. Each clerk can handle at most 20% of the store’s visitors: give both versions enough clerks so nobody goes over that.
n11-canario-4.dica: With 50/50, each side gets half the visitors and splits them among its pods. 50% ÷ 20% = 2.5: round up.
n11-canario-4.vidaReal: Nobody complained: half the visitors already go to the renovation. But a single apartment can’t handle half the condo.
n11-canario-4.limite: The weight splits visitors between the Services, not between the pods: how many pods each side has is your call.

testes.descricao: half on each version, no overloaded clerk

n11-canario-5.enunciado:
1.1 passed the test: it can become the official store. 1.0 leaves the stage, and I don’t want any surprises at the next building maintenance.

Marta, who owns the store

Acceptance criteria. The how is up to you; some of the criteria are checked by hidden tests.

  • Everyone who visits loja.local lands on version 1.1.
  • Nothing of v1 is left in the cluster: no pods, no loja-v1 phone extension.
  • On its own, v2 handles the whole store, with each clerk getting at most 20% of the visitors.
  • A maintenance (the kubectl drain of a building) never leaves the store with fewer than 4 ready clerks.
n11-canario-5.dica: Delete v1.yaml and take v1 out of the route. 100% ÷ 20% = 5 replicas. For the maintenance, a PodDisruptionBudget with v2’s selector (like in the Zero-downtime deploy project).
n11-canario-5.vidaReal: The renovation was approved: everyone moves to the new apartments, the old ones close, and the building maintenance can’t catch the store off guard.
n11-canario-5.limite: Once v1 is deleted, going back means bringing v1 up again: keep its YAML until you’re sure.

testes.descricao: everyone on version 1.1, and nothing of v1
v2 handles the store on its own
the maintenance doesn’t take the store down

msgs.1: a PodDisruptionBudget guarantees at least 4 ready

n11-bf-1.enunciado: hpa.yaml already has the manager’s rules (from 2 to 8 clerks, a 50% CPU target), but kubectl get hpa shows cpu: <unknown>/50%. Find out why (kubectl describe hpa loja) and fix it: the store reserves (requests) 100m of CPU and 64Mi of memory, and can draw at most (limits) 500m and 128Mi.
n11-bf-1.dica: The describe says: missing request for cpu. resources: { requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi }, limits: { cpu: 500m, memory: 128Mi } }
n11-bf-1.vidaReal: The temp-staff manager (the HPA) calls in reinforcements when the clerks go past half their capacity. Except nobody told them what each clerk’s capacity is.
n11-bf-1.limite: The HPA’s percentage is of the request, not of the machine: a made-up request gives a made-up percentage.

testes.descricao: the manager sees the CPU

msgs.4: the HPA measures the CPU (no more <unknown>)

n11-bf-2.enunciado: trafego.yaml has the carga (load) pod, a client that hits the store nonstop, but the address is wrong (check its logs). Fix it and watch the HPA grow (kubectl get hpa -w, with about +30s).
n11-bf-2.dica: kubectl logs carga (bad address). The Service is named loja: http://loja
n11-bf-2.vidaReal: Customers pour in: the manager sees the clerks at their limit and calls in the temps.
n11-bf-2.limite: The HPA reacts, it doesn’t predict: the first minutes of the sale still catch the store small.

testes.descricao: the manager hired temps

msgs.1: the HPA asked for more than 2 replicas

n11-bf-3.enunciado: The management office put a cap on the company’s consumption: apply the teto (cap) quota from cota.yaml, without touching it. With it, kubectl apply starts rejecting one of your pods. Read the error and fix the pod (the values are up to you, as long as they fit under the cap).
n11-bf-3.dica: The error says what’s missing (must specify ...): with a CPU and memory quota, every container has to say how much it asks for. For carga, 50m and 16Mi of request and 100m and 32Mi of limit are enough. kubectl applies the files in alphabetical order: the quota (cota.yaml) arrives before the pod.
n11-bf-3.vidaReal: The management office put a cap on the company’s power: and, with a cap, every appliance that comes in needs an energy label.
n11-bf-3.limite: The quota turns away anything that arrives without a label, even the test client: that’s why it usually comes together with a LimitRange.

testes.descricao: everything under the cap

n11-bf-4.enunciado: relatorio.yaml starts the relatorio (report) pod, which keeps crashing and restarting. Find out the reason and fix it, giving it what it needs without blowing the company’s cap.
n11-bf-4.dica: kubectl describe pod relatorio: Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled. The logs say how much it loads (300Mi): limits.memory has to go above that, with some headroom (384Mi or 512Mi).
n11-bf-4.vidaReal: The Black Friday report loads the whole spreadsheet into memory. Its circuit breaker was sized for a light bulb, and it trips every time.
n11-bf-4.limite: Memory doesn’t stretch: past the limit, the container dies on the spot (OOMKilled). CPU above the limit only makes the container slower.

testes.descricao: the report runs without crashing

n11-bf-5.enunciado:
Every team that arrives here forgets to say how much it consumes, and the quota turns it away. I want a default for whoever arrives without a label, and a limit so nobody plugs in an appliance that’s too big.

Sônia, from the management office

Acceptance criteria. The how is up to you; some of the criteria are checked by hidden tests.

  • The tarefa (task) pod (tarefa.yaml, which you can not change) gets in and runs.
  • Every container that arrives without resources gets 50m of CPU and 32Mi of memory as request, and 100m and 64Mi as limit.
  • No container can have more than 512Mi of memory limit: a bigger request is rejected on the spot.
  • Everything keeps running: the store grows under load, and the report doesn’t crash.
n11-bf-5.dica: A LimitRange (type: Container) does all three: defaultRequest, default and max. It has to exist before the pod, and kubectl applies the files in alphabetical order.
n11-bf-5.vidaReal: So it doesn’t turn away whoever forgets the label, the management office sticks a default label on anyone who arrives without one, and bans appliances that are too big.
n11-bf-5.limite: The default only applies to new pods: those already running don’t get the label.

testes.descricao: the task got the default and got in
a container that’s too big is rejected

msgs.0: a pod with a 1Gi memory limit is rejected

testes.descricao: the store grows and the report runs

msgs.0: the HPA asked for more than 2 replicas

n11-equipes-1.enunciado: andares.yaml creates the time-a and time-b namespaces, and time-a.yaml puts team A’s API on its floor. time-b.yaml has team B’s API, but it doesn’t show up in time-b. Find out where it ended up and fix it.
n11-equipes-1.dica: kubectl get deploy -A shows every floor. Without metadata.namespace (and without -n), everything goes to the default namespace.
n11-equipes-1.vidaReal: Each team rents a floor (the namespace), with its own API and its own phone extension. Team B’s move ended up on the ground floor.
n11-equipes-1.limite: A floor alone doesn’t isolate anything: without badges and turnstiles, anyone can walk all over.

testes.descricao: each team on its own floor

msgs.3: nothing of team B was left in default

n11-equipes-2.enunciado: crachas.yaml has the dev Role and ana’s RoleBinding, in time-a. bruno needs the same role in time-b. Instead of copying the Role onto each floor, turn it into a ClusterRole dev and give each of them the role only on their own floor.
n11-equipes-2.dica: kind: ClusterRole (no namespace) with the same rules; the RoleBindings dev-ana (time-a) and dev-bruno (time-b) with roleRef { kind: ClusterRole, name: dev }. Not a ClusterRoleBinding: that one applies to the whole cluster.
n11-equipes-2.vidaReal: ana has the dev badge for floor A; bruno needs the same one for floor B. Instead of copying the job description onto each floor, the management office writes the job once and hands out badges per floor.
n11-equipes-2.limite: What limits the badge is the binding: a RoleBinding only applies on its own floor, even when it points to a ClusterRole. A ClusterRoleBinding would open every floor.

testes.descricao: a single role, and each one on their own floor

n11-equipes-3.enunciado: carla, from the on-call shift, needs to see pods, logs and the rest on both floors, without being able to change anything and without seeing the Secrets. Don’t write any role: Kubernetes already comes with the view ClusterRole, which does exactly that. Give her that role on both floors, and only there.
n11-equipes-3.dica: A RoleBinding on each floor, with roleRef { kind: ClusterRole, name: view }. Check: kubectl auth can-i get pods --subresource=log -n time-b --as carla.
n11-equipes-3.vidaReal: carla, from the late-night on-call shift, needs to look at everything on both floors (pods, logs, events) to wake up the right person. Touching, no.
n11-equipes-3.limite: The ready-made view role doesn’t read Secrets (passwords aren’t on-call business): if she needs a Secret, that’s another badge.

testes.descricao: carla looks at both floors and touches nothing

n11-equipes-4.enunciado: catracas.yaml closes each floor to outsiders, and clientes.yaml puts a client on each floor for testing. But the penetration test showed that the time-a client still reaches the api on time-b. Find the leak and close it, without closing the floor to its own residents.
n11-equipes-4.dica: Compare the two so-o-andar policies (kubectl describe netpol -A). namespaceSelector: {} picks every namespace; podSelector: {} on its own picks the pods in the policy’s own namespace.
n11-equipes-4.vidaReal: Each floor’s turnstiles were supposed to let in only people from that same floor. Floor B’s has a leak.
n11-equipes-4.limite: Whoever has the floor’s badge (RBAC) can change its turnstiles: turnstiles are network, badges are API.

testes.descricao: each one on their own floor

n11-equipes-5.enunciado:
Team A is going to use our API. But only their client, which is the program that knows the contract: no random pod from floor A knocking on our door.

Bruno, from team B

Acceptance criteria. The how is up to you; some of the criteria are checked by hidden tests.

  • The cliente on time-a (label app: cliente) calls the api on time-b.
  • No other pod on time-a reaches the api on time-b (the curioso (nosy) pod, from visitas.yaml, for example).
  • time-b still can’t reach the api on time-a, and inside each floor everything keeps working.
n11-equipes-5.dica: In a from rule, two items (- namespaceSelector and - podSelector) mean OR; namespaceSelector and podSelector in the same item mean AND. For the namespace, the kubernetes.io/metadata.name: time-a label comes for free.
n11-equipes-5.vidaReal: Team B opens its API’s door to team A’s client program, and only to it.
n11-equipes-5.limite: The turnstile trusts labels: anyone who can create pods on floor A with app: cliente gets through too. That’s why the badge (RBAC) and the turnstile go together.

testes.descricao: only the time-a client reaches the time-b API
everything else stays as it was

n11-cofre-1.titulo: The safe without the master key
n11-cofre-1.enunciado: They asked for cofre (the safe) to never run as root, and someone put runAsNonRoot: true on the pod. Since then, it won’t start. Find out why and make the safe run as user 1000, without removing the lock.
n11-cofre-1.dica: The pod’s events (kubectl describe pod) say: container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root. The busybox image runs as root: say which user to use (runAsUser: 1000, in the pod’s securityContext).
n11-cofre-1.vidaReal: The safe’s program runs with an ordinary resident’s key, never with the master key.
n11-cofre-1.limite: Running without root limits the damage, but it doesn’t replace updating the image with the security fixes.

testes.descricao: the safe runs as 1000

n11-cofre-2.enunciado: bloco.yaml creates the cofre namespace, with the fire marshals’ restricted code. Move the safe into that namespace. It’s going to be turned away: find out what the code requires and meet all of it.
n11-cofre-2.dica: The apply warns you (Warning: would violate PodSecurity), and the ReplicaSet’s events say what’s missing: kubectl get events -n cofre. There are three fields: allowPrivilegeEscalation, capabilities and seccompProfile.
n11-cofre-2.vidaReal: The safe moves into the block with the fire marshals’ strictest code: at the front gate, the inspector reads the list of requirements and turns away whoever doesn’t comply.
n11-cofre-2.limite: The code only checks new pods: an old pod, created before the label, keeps running.

testes.descricao: the safe passed the fire marshals’ inspection

n11-cofre-3.enunciado: The audit asks for the container’s disk to be read-only (readOnlyRootFilesystem: true). Turn the lock on, and the safe will start crashing. Find out why and fix it without turning the lock off.
n11-cofre-3.dica: kubectl logs -n cofre deploy/cofre: the program writes to /tmp when it starts. Give it a workbench: an emptyDir volume mounted at /tmp.
n11-cofre-3.vidaReal: The safe’s walls stay sealed; the program only writes on the workbench (/tmp).
n11-cofre-3.limite: /tmp is an emptyDir: whatever is there disappears when the pod goes away.

testes.descricao: the safe runs, and the workbench accepts writes
the walls don’t

n11-cofre-4.enunciado: segredo.yaml keeps the safe’s combinacao (combination) (a Secret in the cofre namespace). The audit robot, the auditor ServiceAccount in the cofre namespace (which doesn’t exist yet), needs to read that Secret, and only that one: no other Secret, not the list of them, and no changes.
n11-cofre-4.dica: The auditor ServiceAccount, a Role with verbs: [get], resources: [secrets] and resourceNames: [combinacao], and the RoleBinding tying the two together. The cofre namespace comes from bloco.yaml, and kubectl applies the files in alphabetical order. Check: kubectl auth can-i get secret/combinacao -n cofre --as system:serviceaccount:cofre:auditor.
n11-cofre-4.vidaReal: The auditor gets a badge that opens a single drawer of the safe, the one with the combination. The other drawers, and the list of them, stay closed to them.
n11-cofre-4.limite: resourceNames doesn’t work for list or watch: the list shows every name, so whoever can only see one drawer can’t list.

testes.descricao: the auditor reads the combination, and only that

n11-cofre-5.enunciado:
Last item in the report: the safe is plugged into the condo’s network like any other apartment. I left a neighbor to check (vizinho.yaml, with a test phone extension for the safe).

Ivo, from the audit team

Acceptance criteria. The how is up to you; some of the criteria are checked by hidden tests.

  • Nobody from outside the cofre namespace opens a connection to the safe (the vizinho (neighbor) tries through the test extension, cofre.cofre).
  • The safe doesn’t open a connection to anyone (not even to the vizinho, in default), but it can still look up names in DNS.
  • The safe doesn’t carry the API token: it never talks to the management office.
  • Everything the audit already approved stays: the restricted code, user 1000 and the read-only disk.
n11-cofre-5.dica: A NetworkPolicy with policyTypes [Ingress, Egress] and no rules closes both doors; the way out to DNS opens with an egress rule to port 53 (UDP and TCP) of kube-dns, in kube-system. The token: automountServiceAccountToken: false on the pod. For busybox’s nslookup, use the full name (vizinho.default.svc.cluster.local).
n11-cofre-5.vidaReal: The safe sits in a room with no windows: nobody gets in, it doesn’t get out, and the only wire plugged in is the phone directory’s (DNS).
n11-cofre-5.limite: The turnstile only looks at the network: whoever has a badge for kubectl exec still gets into the safe through the management office.

testes.descricao: nobody gets into the safe

msgs.1: the neighbor can’t open a connection to the safe

testes.descricao: the safe doesn’t get out, but finds names

msgs.0: the safe’s wget to the neighbor doesn’t complete
msgs.1: the safe’s nslookup finds the neighbor

testes.descricao: the safe doesn’t carry the API token

msgs.0: the safe’s pod doesn’t mount the token (no kube-api-access among the volumes)

testes.descricao: what was already approved stays

n11-ambientes-1.enunciado: dev.yaml has the dev values. From the terminal, install the loja-dev release of kube-learn/loja with them, in the dev namespace (which doesn’t exist yet).
n11-ambientes-1.dica: helm install loja-dev kube-learn/loja -f dev.yaml -n dev --create-namespace
n11-ambientes-1.vidaReal: The builder’s same standard design, with each city’s finishes in a file.
n11-ambientes-1.limite: Each environment’s values.yaml is code: keep it in git, along with everything else.

testes.descricao: the dev store

n11-ambientes-1.projeto: Helm and Kustomize, dev and prod

n11-ambientes-2.enunciado: Now prod. The value names are in the chart itself (helm show values kube-learn/loja): complete prod.yaml with 3 replicas, the tag "1.1", the Ingress turned on with the host loja.prod and each pod reserving 100m of CPU. Install the loja-prod release in the prod namespace.
n11-ambientes-2.dica: replicaCount, image.tag, ingress: { enabled: true, host: loja.prod } and resources: { requests: { cpu: 100m } }. helm install loja-prod kube-learn/loja -f prod.yaml -n prod --create-namespace
n11-ambientes-2.vidaReal: The big branch: more clerks, the new version, a desk out on the street and reserved power.
n11-ambientes-2.limite: Two values files drift apart over time: whatever doesn’t need to differ, leave it at the chart’s defaults.

testes.descricao: the prod store

n11-ambientes-2.projeto: Helm and Kustomize, dev and prod

n11-ambientes-3.enunciado: In staging (the loja release, in the default namespace), someone ran an upgrade, and the new store keeps crashing. From the terminal, find out what changed and roll the release back to the last revision that worked, without uninstalling anything.
n11-ambientes-3.dica: helm history loja shows the revisions; helm get values loja --revision 2 shows what changed. To go back: helm rollback loja 1.
n11-ambientes-3.vidaReal: At the test branch, someone swapped the finishes for a defective batch. The builder keeps every version of the design: you can go back to the previous one.
n11-ambientes-3.limite: The rollback creates a new revision with the old values; it doesn’t erase the history, and the defective revision stays there for anyone who wants to investigate.

testes.descricao: staging is back

n11-ambientes-3.projeto: Helm and Kustomize, dev and prod

n11-ambientes-4.enunciado: The base/ folder has the store’s Deployment and Service, and the overlays/dev overlay uses the base. But kubectl apply -k overlays/dev only creates the namespace. Make the dev store really come up: the base reads its variables from the loja-config ConfigMap, which the dev overlay has to generate with COR=amarelo.
n11-ambientes-4.dica: base/kustomization.yaml lists nothing under resources: list deployment.yaml and service.yaml. In the overlay: configMapGenerator: [{ name: loja-config, literals: [COR=amarelo] }]. Look at the result before applying: kubectl kustomize overlays/dev.
n11-ambientes-4.vidaReal: Another team prefers the common blueprint with adjustment sheets: the base is plain YAML, and each sheet generates its own environment’s bulletin board.
n11-ambientes-4.limite: The generator adds a hash to the ConfigMap’s name (loja-config-abc123) and swaps the reference in the Deployment: change the color, the name changes, and the pods are recreated.

testes.descricao: dev comes up, yellow

n11-ambientes-4.projeto: Helm and Kustomize, dev and prod

n11-ambientes-5.enunciado:
The Kustomize team wants the prod environment too. Same base, no copying YAML: whatever changes in prod lives in prod’s sheet.

Léo, from the platform team

Acceptance criteria. The how is up to you; some of the criteria are checked by hidden tests.

  • kubectl apply -k overlays/prod puts everything in the prod-k namespace.
  • Prod runs 3 pods of kubelearn/loja:1.1, with COR=azul.
  • Each prod pod reserves 100m of CPU and 64Mi of memory.
  • The base doesn’t change: dev still has 1 pod of 1.0, yellow, with no reservation at all.
n11-ambientes-5.dica: In the prod overlay: namespace, replicas, images (newTag) and configMapGenerator, like in dev; the reservation comes in through a patch (patches) that only prod applies.
n11-ambientes-5.vidaReal: The big branch’s adjustment sheet: its neighborhood, more clerks, the new version, its own color and reserved power.
n11-ambientes-5.limite: Overlays only see the base: an adjustment everyone wants goes in the base, not copied into every sheet.

testes.descricao: prod: 3 pods of 1.1, blue
prod reserves CPU and memory
dev stays as it was

n11-ambientes-5.projeto: Helm and Kustomize, dev and prod

n11-licao-proximos-passos.enunciado:
Everything you did here works on a real cluster: the commands and the YAMLs are the same. Three ways to get started, from the simplest to the most complete:

Killercoda (in the browser)

A real cluster, free, for an hour, with nothing to install: killercoda.com/playgrounds. Good for redoing the missions from here with real containers.

kind (on your computer)

The same one that checked this site’s outputs: a cluster inside Docker.

# with Docker installed
kind create cluster --name estudo
kubectl get nodes
kubectl apply -f loja.yaml
kind delete cluster --name estudo

For 3 nodes like here, a config file with one control-plane and two worker.

minikube

Another local cluster, with ready-made extras (minikube addons enable metrics-server, minikube dashboard). Watch out for the ingress addon: it installs ingress-nginx, retired in 2026 (level 3). For the front gate, prefer the Gateway API: install its CRDs and an implementation, such as Envoy Gateway or Traefik.

Where to go next

  • The official documentation: kubernetes.io/docs.
  • If you want a certification, the CKAD covers almost everything on this path (the exam is hands-on, in a terminal, with access to the documentation).
  • Build your own project: take an application of yours and write the manifests from scratch. That’s where you see what you’ve learned.

Thanks for coming aboard. The ship is fully loaded. 🚢
n11-licao-proximos-passos.vidaReal: You trained in the model condo. Now it’s time to visit a real construction site: the same kubectl, the same YAMLs, only with real containers running.
n11-licao-proximos-passos.limite: The simulator mimicked kubectl’s output against a real kind, but it’s a simulator: on a real cluster, images take time, networks fail in new ways and errors don’t come with an explanation underneath.
